title: UV Protection Without Irritation—Meet the Best Sunscreens for Sensitive Skin - Vogue

 By Iman Balagam and Jenny Berg October 30, 2026 Photo: Courtesy of Ingu Chen and Fujio Emura Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story The rules have changed when it comes to choosing the best sunscreens for sensitive skin. In the past, mineral or nontoxic was the way to go for those prone to breakouts or irritation. These days, the playing field has widened considerably, with gentle chemical formulas and K-beauty options designed to pamper and protect the skin.
 Vogue ’s Favorite Sunscreens for Sensitive Skin:
 Best Overall: Elta MD UV Clear Sunscreen , $42
 Best With BEMT: La Roche-Posay Anthelios UVDefense Sunscreen SPF 50 , $40
 Best Drugstore: Neutrogena Ultra Sheer Face Liquid Mineral Sunscreen , $14
 Best for Sensitive Skin: Avène Mineral Sunscreen Multi-Defense Fluid , $38
 Best for Hydration: Round Lab Birch Juice Moisturizing UVLock Spectrum 45 Sunscreen , $28
 Best Splurge: SkinCeuticals Physical Fusion UV Defense , $45
 “Overall, sunscreens for sensitive skin are improving both in terms of efficacy and cosmetic elegance,” says Marisa Garshick, MD , a board-certified dermatologist in Manhattan and New Jersey. “Newer mineral formulations have been developed that are lightweight, absorb easily, and are not as likely to leave behind a white cast.” Plus, the newly FDA-approved SPF filter bemotrizinol ( BEMT ) has expanded the options for those with sensitive skin who prefer a chemical formula.
 “BEMT may not be as likely to cause a reaction as some other chemical filters,” Dr. Garshick notes. “It is a large molecule that does not have as much systemic or skin absorption, which may lower the potential risk of skin irritation.” Additionally, the synthetic organic UV filter is photostable, so it may not require the addition of other stabilizing chemicals that can trigger a reaction in some sensitive skin types.
 Overall, Dr. Garshick says, the new class of sunscreens are formulated with daily use in mind, rather than an occasional day at the beach. Incorporating hydrating ingredients like hyaluronic acid and glycerin, plus calming ingredients like niacinamide, the modern formulas minimize the potential for dryness and irritation in sensitive skin—and they’re more enjoyable to use. Ahead, find the soothing formulas that dermatologists and Vogue editors trust to keep UV damage (and breakouts and redness) at bay.

 Best Overall: EltaMD UV Clear Sunscreen
 Save to wishlist Save to wishlist EltaMD
 UV Clear Sunscreen
 $46 AMAZON
 Why We Love It: You’d be hard-pressed to find a dermatologist who doesn’t rave about this sunscreen. Its lightweight formula glides on easily with no white cast, and it helps soothe sensitive skin types prone to acne, rosacea, and hyperpigmentation. Board-certified dermatologist Onyeka Obioha-Lolagne describes it as her go-to: “This sunscreen blends in well with all skin tones, including deep skin tones, and also contains niacinamide—a potent antioxidant with anti-inflammatory properties.” Plus, it’s oil-free, making it ideal for those with oily, acne-prone skin. The formula has another fan in Blair Murphy Rose, MD, a New York City–based board-certified dermatologist. “I frequently recommend UV Clear to my acne-prone or oily skin patients for excellent sun protection that won’t promote breakouts,” Dr. Rose previously said . "My patients love it! [This] is noncomedogenic and formulated with lactic acid and niacinamide to prevent acne and reduce inflammation.”

 Best Mineral Sunscreen: SkinCeuticals Physical Fusion UV Defense
 Save to wishlist Save to wishlist SkinCeuticals
 Physical Fusion UV Defense
 $45 BLUEMERCURY
 Why We Love It: Have a winter escape planned? If you’re heading to the beach or pool, you’ll need something water-resistant like this one from SkinCeuticals, which is effective for up to 40 minutes. It glides on easily with no white cast, leaving behind a gorgeous natural tint so you can skip the base makeup. Dr. Obioha-Lolagne is also a fan: “This mineral sunscreen is oil-free and fragrance-free. It contains iron oxide, providing a tint to the formula and protecting against visible light, which may contribute to unwanted hyperpigmentation,” she says. Just heed this advice: “Water-resistant” is not “waterproof.” Basically, the term means that if you get splashed with water, the sunscreen won’t instantly come off. But if you’re paddling around in a pool for longer than 40 minutes, it will. As always with sunscreen, reapplication of water-resistant formulas is key—and physical sun protection never hurts in a beach or poolside setting.

 Anthelios UV Defense SPF
 $40 AMAZON
 Why We Love It: This French pharmacy staple boasts La Roche-Posay’s signature Cell-Ox Shield Technology, which pairs a UV filter with an antioxidant complex. As for that UV filter, “This formula incorporates bemotrizinol (BEMT), the newest broad-spectrum filter that may help deliver effective protection in a lightweight, cosmetically elegant texture,” Dr. Garshick says. She’s also on board with the sensorial experience. Infused with glycerin and vitamin E, “it offers a lightweight, milky feel that feels hydrating and absorbs easily, making it a great option for all skin types—including those with sensitive skin,” she says. One caveat: Before applying any new product or ingredient on sensitive skin, Dr. Garshick recommends patch-testing it first.
 Editor’s Experience: “I trust any La Roche-Posay sunscreen, and this one didn’t disappoint. My favorite part is its texture; it’s an incredibly lightweight, milky lotion that absorbs quickly into my skin and leaves it feeling really soft. It’s also super hydrating, which is always a nice added bonus, and it just feels so much better on my skin than a lot of the US sunscreens I’ve been wearing lately. I’ll definitely be adding this to my daily skin-care routine, and when people ask me for recs, I’ll be mentioning this.” —Audrey Noble, contributor

 Why We Love It: With an SPF of 70, it’s clear that Neutrogena is aiming to compete with some of the most protective formulas on the market. (SPF 70 theoretically allows you to stay in the sun 70 times longer without burning.) Dr. Ruth says, “I recommend this for patients looking for a lightweight, fragrance-free formula that layers well under makeup.” Its mineral-only filter is gentle on sensitive or acne-prone skin, making this noncomedogenic SPF formula less likely to cause breakouts. The liquid sunscreen has an ultralight texture and a silky feel. Though it’s known to leave less of a white cast on the skin than some other mineral formulas, the brand notes that layering the SPF on top of a moisturizer or under a foundation can help it blend in even more easily.

 Why We Love It: Just what the doctor ordered, this modern facial sunscreen features a microdispersion delivery system that provides a melting effect for ease of application and better absorption. According to board-certified dermatologist Dr. Ava Shamban, its combination of zinc oxide and titanium dioxide is safe for sensitive skin types. “The formulation is very skin-centric and helps to strengthen the skin barrier. Vitamin E is a great antioxidant to support protection, while peptides enhance skin structure and elasticity. Brightening agents like carrot root and extract are an added bonus,” she says. Dr. Garshick calls the zinc-based sunscreen “a good option” for sensitive skin as it’s fragrance-free, and says that its infusion of peptides and vitamin E makes it ideal for daily use. Still, “since there are some botanical extracts, it is important for someone with sensitive skin to patch-test before use to ensure no sensitivity,” she notes.

It combines pure zinc oxide with key moisturizing and antioxidant factors to further protect, correct, and nourish the skin. “Heart leaf and rice bran oil are less common but are equally effective in soothing and supporting skin protection,” she adds. According to Dr. Garshick: “This mineral-based broad-spectrum sunscreen also helps hydrate the skin while leaving a satin finish behind. It contains ceramides, hyaluronic acid, and niacinamide to hydrate the skin, making it a good option for those with sensitive skin.”

 Everything You Need to Know 
 What type of sunscreen is best for sensitive skin?
 AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron The experts are in agreement that if you have sensitive skin, you should stick with mineral sunscreen. “Mineral sunscreen contains no chemicals that frequently cause irritation and allergic reactions in the skin,” explains Dr. Greenfield. Minerals sit on top of the skin and provide broad-spectrum sunscreen coverage against all wavelengths of UVA and UVB light while avoiding common skin reactions and rashes.
 More specifically, according to Dr. Obioha-Lolagne, you’ll want to look for mineral sunscreen with zinc oxide and/or titanium dioxide in the formula, “the reason being that those with sensitive skin are more likely to have allergic reactions to the active ingredients in chemical sunscreens than to those in mineral sunscreens.”
 What to Look For in a Sunscreen for Sensitive Skin
 AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Chemical Vs. Mineral 
 For sensitive skin, Dr. King generally recommends mineral sunscreens as well. These often include humectants and noncomedogenic emollients in their base formulas, which help keep the skin moisturized and prevent pore clogging.
 SPF Level 
 According to Dr. Greenfield, SPF should be 30+ (minimum) for the face, and mineral sunscreens provide broad-spectrum protection.
 Key Ingredients 
 Protection doesn’t mean you have to compromise on hydration. “Look for moisturizing ingredients such as ceramides, squalene, and hyaluronic acid to enhance skin hydration and avoid leaving the skin chalky with a white cast,” says Dr. Obioha-Lolagne.
 If breakouts are your main concern, King notes, two factors can cause sunscreen-related breakouts: occlusion of the pores by comedogenic materials, or a sensitivity reaction to chemical UV-blocking ingredients. Breakouts can result from any ingredient in the product, not just the active sunscreen components. Other emollients, fragrances, preservatives, or additional ingredients can also cause breakouts. Look for “noncomedogenic” on the label. Zinc oxide and titanium dioxide are both noncomedogenic.
 King also warns to be wary of expiration dates. If the sunscreen has expired or the ingredients have been exposed to direct sunlight and high temperatures, the heat and sun can break down the chemicals, rendering them ineffective and potentially irritating to the skin.
 Texture 
 Dr. Greenfield advises that the texture should be light and breathable to avoid clogging pores or causing breakouts, yet thick enough to stay on the skin and not rub off easily. Lotions, creams, and gels are preferred over sprays, which can result in skipped areas.
 Should I wear sunscreen if I have sensitive skin?
 AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Absolutely! Dr. Greenfield emphasizes, “It’s perfectly fine to have a little sun exposure on your body, but UV radiation will only cause accelerated aging, discoloration, and texture changes on your face. I recommend facial sunscreen every single day, rain or shine.”
 Is SPF 50 too much for sensitive skin?
 AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron According to Dr. Shambam, the amount of SPF is not the primary factor for sensitive skin; rather, it’s the type of chemicals, actives, or ingredients that often cause reactivity. Products with higher percentages of chemical actives can be more aggressive and lead to irritation. Dr. Shambam explains that while using a sunscreen with SPF 50 is perfectly fine, the difference in protection between SPF 30 and SPF 50 is minimal, and even less so between SPF 30 and SPF 70 or higher. A quality broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 blocks 95%–97% of UV rays. She adds, “For the most sensitive or reactive skin types, it's important to read the labels, be aware of key ingredients, and look for products specifically labeled for sensitive skin.”
 What sunscreen should you use if you’re allergic to the sun?
 AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron “Zinc oxide and titanium-dioxide-based sunscreens are usually the best and most effective options to prevent allergic reactions when in the sun,” Dr. Shambam says. However, she does advise patients who are allergic to the sun to do their best to avoid exposure when possible. When that’s not feasible, UPF clothing, hats, and umbrellas are always recommended.
 Meet the Experts
 AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Dr. Onyeka Obioha-Lolagne is a board-certified dermatologist and owner of Boutik Dermatology in Beverly Hills
 Dr. Marisa Garshick is a leading board-certified dermatologist at MDCS Dermatology, as well as an assistant clinical professor of dermatology at Cornell - New York Presbyterian Medical Center.
 Dr. Nava Greenfield is a board-certified dermatologist at Schweiger Dermatology Group in New York
 Dr. Hadley King is a New York City–based board-certified dermatologist
 Katie Mellinger is a bicoastal makeup artist living in both Los Angeles and New York
 Dr. Ava Shamban is a board-certified dermatologist living in both Santa Monica and Beverly Hills and the founder of Ava MD and Skin Five .
 Dr. Nicole Ruth is a board-certified dermatologist based in New York.
